slides.title: Sodium (Na)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: A routine test of general health that helps find and monitor conditions affecting the balance of fluids, electrolytes and acidity. It is often done as part of an electrolyte panel or a basic (BMP) or comprehensive (CMP) metabolic panel.

It may be ordered at a routine checkup, in people taking medicines that can affect fluid balance, or when there are symptoms of high sodium (thirst, passing very little urine) or low sodium (weakness, fatigue). Confusion, muscle twitching and seizures can occur with both.
Sodium is often measured with other electrolytes for the anion gap test, which looks at the difference between negatively and positively charged electrolytes and helps check for acid imbalances.

slides.title: Sodium (Na)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Sodium is an electrolyte: it helps control the amount of body fluid and the acid–base (pH) balance, and helps nerves and muscles work properly. Most sodium comes from the diet; the kidneys excrete any excess in urine, and blood sodium is normally kept within a very narrow range.

slides.title: Sodium (Na)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: Possible causes of a higher-than-normal result include dehydration (from not drinking enough, diarrhea or diuretic medicines), adrenal gland disorders, kidney disease and, uncommonly, diabetes insipidus.

Low: Possible causes include sodium loss through diarrhea or vomiting, and conditions in which the body holds onto extra fluid that dilutes sodium: kidney disease, cirrhosis of the liver, heart failure, certain brain and lung diseases, some cancers and certain medicines (including many over-the-counter pain relievers and some antidepressants). Addison disease and malnutrition are also listed.

slides.title: Sodium (Na)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines being taken; some may need to be stopped before the test, but only on the provider’s instruction. Fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

Limitations: A result outside the normal range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment: certain medicines, age, sex and some medical conditions can raise or lower sodium. For diagnosis, the result is usually considered together with other tests, such as other electrolytes.

slides.title: Potassium (K)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)

What it is used for: Often part of a routine electrolyte panel; used to diagnose or monitor conditions linked to abnormal potassium, such as kidney disease, high blood pressure and heart disease. It is also used to monitor diabetes, kidney disease or adrenal gland disorders and people taking medicines that can affect potassium.

Physiology: Potassium is an electrolyte that cells, nerves, the heart and muscles need to work properly. Almost all body potassium is inside cells, with only a small amount in the blood; the kidneys remove potassium in urine to keep the blood level right.

slides.title: Potassium (K)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: High potassium (hyperkalemia) often has two or more causes. Possibilities include kidney disease, Addison disease, injuries, burns or surgery (which make cells release extra potassium), poorly controlled type 1 diabetes, side effects of certain medicines such as diuretics or antibiotics and, uncommonly, a very high potassium intake from food or supplements.

Low: Possible causes of low potassium (hypokalemia) include side effects of prescription diuretics, fluid loss from diarrhea, vomiting or heavy sweating, laxative overuse, adrenal gland disorders (Cushing’s syndrome, aldosteronism), kidney disease, alcohol use disorder and, uncommonly, a diet too low in potassium.

slides.title: Potassium (K)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a potassium test or an electrolyte panel. Fasting for several hours may be needed if other tests are ordered on the same blood sample.
Interferences: Repeatedly clenching and relaxing the fist just before or during blood collection can temporarily raise blood potassium and lead to an incorrect result.

Certain prescription and over-the-counter medicines and supplements may raise potassium. Natural black licorice should not be eaten for at least two weeks before the test because it may lower potassium.
Limitations: A result outside the normal range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Calcium (Ca)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used to check general health and to help diagnose or monitor conditions affecting the bones, kidneys, digestive system, thyroid and parathyroid glands. Total calcium is the most common blood calcium test and is often part of the BMP and CMP.

Ionized calcium is harder to measure; it is usually ordered when total calcium is abnormal, when a condition affects the balance of ionized and bound calcium, or in people who are seriously ill or having surgery.

Many people with high or low calcium have no symptoms, so the test may be ordered in known conditions that can affect calcium, such as kidney disease, thyroid or parathyroid disease, malnutrition, problems absorbing calcium and certain cancers.

slides.title: Calcium (Ca)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: About 1% of the body’s calcium is in the blood; the rest is stored in bones and teeth. The right blood calcium level is needed for nerves, muscles and the heart to work properly; calcium also helps blood vessels move blood and helps release hormones.

Blood calcium exists in two forms normally present in about equal amounts: calcium bound to proteins and free (ionized) calcium, the form active in many body functions. Because the body tightly controls their balance, total calcium usually gives a good estimate of ionized calcium.

slides.title: Calcium (Ca)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: Possible causes of high total calcium (hypercalcemia) include overactive parathyroid glands (hyperparathyroidism), certain cancers including cancer that has spread to bone, bone disorders such as Paget’s disease of bone, and taking too much vitamin D over a long period.

Low: Possible causes of low total calcium (hypocalcemia) include low blood protein levels (for example from liver disease or malnutrition), underactive parathyroid glands (hypoparathyroidism), too little dietary calcium, too little vitamin D or magnesium, pancreatitis and kidney disease.

slides.title: Calcium (Ca)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: Usually no special preparation is needed. Tell the provider about all medicines and supplements, such as vitamin D, as some may need to be stopped (only on the provider’s instruction); fasting may be needed if other tests are ordered on the sample.
Interferences: Diet and certain medicines can affect calcium levels, so a total calcium result outside the normal range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.
Limitations: A blood calcium test does not show how much calcium is in the bones; bone mineral content is measured with a bone density (DEXA) scan.

slides.title: Calcium disorders (hyper- and hypocalcemia)
bullets: Many people with high or low calcium have no symptoms. Results are interpreted together with PTH; total calcium usually gives a good estimate of ionized calcium.

slides.title: Calcium disorders (hyper- and hypocalcemia)
rows: Helps diagnose or monitor conditions of the bones, kidneys, digestive system, thyroid and parathyroid glands.
To find out whether a parathyroid disorder is causing abnormal calcium (its most common use); usually ordered with calcium.
Low blood protein (from liver disease or malnutrition) can make total calcium low.
When total calcium is abnormal, when calcium balance is affected, or in seriously ill people.
Too little vitamin D can cause low calcium; too much vitamin D over a long time can cause high calcium.
Too little magnesium can also cause low calcium.
Phosphate is linked to calcium: in hyperparathyroidism calcium is high and phosphate low; in hypoparathyroidism the reverse.
Kidney disease is one cause of low calcium.

slides.title: Calcium disorders (hyper- and hypocalcemia)
rows: Secondary hyperparathyroidism: the cause lies outside the glands — low vitamin D, phosphate or magnesium, too little calcium, poor absorption, or kidney failure.
Hypoparathyroidism is likely (damage from neck surgery or radiation, autoimmune or genetic causes, and others).
Possible hyperparathyroidism, certain cancers (including spread to bone), Paget’s disease of bone, or too much vitamin D over a long time.
Low blood protein may be the reason.

slides.title: Calcium disorders (hyper- and hypocalcemia)
bullets: Diet and certain medicines affect calcium — an out-of-range result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: ~3.5–5.0 (sources differ: 3.6–5.5 mmol/L; lower limit 3.5 mmol/L) mmol/L
adults, non-hemolyzed serum or heparinized plasma
slides.footnote: The reference interval varies by laboratory, method and population; the laboratory verifies its own interval (verification).

slides.title: A patient’s blood sodium is lower than normal. Which possible cause is consistent with the source?
options: Heart failure, which can make the body hold onto extra fluid
Dehydration from not drinking enough fluids over a long period
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source lists conditions that make the body hold onto fluid that dilutes sodium, including heart failure, as possible causes of low sodium.

Basis: Low sodium may reflect sodium loss or fluid retention that dilutes sodium; dehydration and diabetes insipidus are listed among causes of high sodium.

slides.title: A person without complaints has a sodium result slightly outside the normal range. Which statement best reflects the source?
options: Sodium varies widely in healthy people, so the result can be ignored
It does not necessarily mean disease: medicines, age, sex and some conditions can shift sodium, and the result is read together with other tests such as other electrolytes
It confirms kidney disease, because the kidneys control sodium
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source states that an out-of-range result does not always need treatment and that diagnosis uses other test results.

Basis: An out-of-range sodium result is interpreted in context: medicines, age, sex and other test results.

slides.title: A potassium result is unexpectedly high in a patient without complaints. Which collection-related factor named by the source could falsely raise it?
options: Not fasting for several hours before the test
Eating a lot of natural black licorice in the days leading up to the blood test
Repeated fist clenching and relaxing just before or during the blood draw
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source says this may temporarily increase potassium and lead to an incorrect result.

Basis: Fist clenching can temporarily raise potassium; licorice may lower it.

slides.title: Which of the following does the source list as a possible cause of LOW blood potassium?
options: Burns or surgery that make cells release potassium into the blood
Fluid loss from diarrhea, vomiting or heavy sweating
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source lists this as a possible cause of hypokalemia.

Basis: Causes of hypokalemia include diuretics, fluid loss, laxative overuse and adrenal disorders, among others.

slides.title: According to the source, when is an ionized calcium test usually ordered?
options: As the routine first-line calcium screen, because it is the easiest test
To measure how much calcium is stored in the bones
When total calcium is abnormal, when a condition disturbs the bound/ionized balance, or in seriously ill or surgical patients
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source lists exactly these situations.

Basis: Total calcium usually estimates ionized calcium well; ionized calcium is measured in specific situations.

slides.title: A patient with liver disease and low blood protein levels has a low total calcium. Which statement fits the source?
options: Low blood protein is listed as a possible cause of low total calcium; total calcium includes the protein-bound fraction
A low total calcium always means bone calcium is depleted
Low total calcium points to overactive parathyroid glands
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source lists low blood protein (from liver disease or malnutrition) as a cause of hypocalcemia, and total calcium measures all blood calcium, including the protein-bound form.

Basis: Low blood protein is among the causes of hypocalcemia; blood calcium does not reflect bone calcium.

Methods of determining sodium, potassium, chloride. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 1. Sodium is the main extracellular cation (normal ~136–145 mmol/L), determines osmolality and volume; potassium is the main intracellular cation (~3.5–5.0 mmol/L), membrane potential, heart rhythm; chloride is the main anion, acid-base balance.

2. Method – ion-selective electrodes (ISE): direct (undiluted – blood gas analyzers) and indirect (diluted – large biochemistry analyzers); with indirect ISE, hyperlipidemia and hyperproteinemia give false hyponatremia.

3. Potassium preanalytics: hemolysis, fist clenching, prolonged tourniquet, K-EDTA contamination, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis (in serum) give false hyperkalemia – when in doubt remeasure in heparinized plasma; storage in the cold also raises K.
4. Hyponatremia: water excess (SIADH, heart/liver failure), Na loss (diuretics, vomiting, adrenal insufficiency); hypernatremia – water loss, diabetes insipidus.

slides.title: Methods of determining sodium, potassium, chloride. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 5. Hyperkalemia: renal failure, hypoaldosteronism, drugs, cell breakdown, acidosis; hypokalemia: diuretics, vomiting/diarrhea, hyperaldosteronism, alkalosis.
6. Chloride: falls in metabolic alkalosis (vomiting), rises in hyperchloremic acidosis; used in interpreting the anion gap (Na − (Cl + HCO3)).

slides.title: Methods of determining calcium, phosphorus. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 1. Calcium in the blood occurs in three forms: ionized (~half, biologically active), protein-bound (mainly albumin) and complexed with anions; total calcium by photometric methods, ionized by ISE.
2. Albumin correction: corrected Ca (mg/dL) = Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin g/dL); when albumin or pH changes, measuring ionized calcium is preferable; normal about 8.8–10.4 mg/dL (2.2–2.6 mmol/L).
3. Hypercalcemia: primary hyperparathyroidism (PTH high), tumors (PTHrP, osteolytic metastases), vitamin D excess; work-up – PTH, PTHrP, 25(OH)D.
4. Hypocalcemia: hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, CKD, magnesium deficiency, acute pancreatitis; first correct for albumin.
5. Phosphorus (phosphate) is determined photometrically; hyperphosphatemia – renal failure, hypoparathyroidism; hypophosphatemia – hyperparathyroidism, malnutrition; hemolysis distorts the result.

slides.title: Methods of determining calcium, clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 1. Total calcium – photometric methods on automated analyzers (colored complex with a metallochromogen); the result is interpreted together with albumin.
2. Ionized calcium – ISE (blood gas analyzers), anaerobic sample, pH-dependent; preferable when albumin changes.
3. Albumin correction: Ca (mg/dL) + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin, g/dL); normal ~8.8–10.4 mg/dL.
4. Hypercalcemia: primary hyperparathyroidism, tumors, vitamin D intoxication, granulomatous diseases; hypocalcemia: hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, CKD, hypomagnesemia, pancreatitis.
5. Preanalytics: prolonged tourniquet (false increase), EDTA/citrate/oxalate tubes (false decrease), hemolysis.
